The Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad.
"May we hear with our ears what is auspicious"—thus the Peace invocation.
Chapter One.
The Instruction on the Eight Limbs of Yoga:
Śāṇḍilya indeed asked Atharvan, "Please explain the eight-limbed yoga which is the means for attaining the Self. He [replied]: 1. He...

Atharvan said: "Restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi) are the eight limbs. Among these, there are ten restraints, likewise ten observances, eight postures, three types of breath control, five withdrawals of the senses, and likewise—
The dhāraṇās; meditation is of two kinds; but concentration is of a single form. || 3 ||
He whose awakening leads those practitioners of the eight-limbed yoga— beginning with Yama— as taught in the Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad, to absolute liberation (kaivalya), that Rāma is my supreme goal.

Indeed, this Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad, which is a division of the Atharvaveda, unfolds here, intent upon revealing the eight-limbed yoga beginning with *yama*, along with its secondary and primary accomplishments, culminating in the non-dual Brahman alone. Of this [Upaniṣad]...
(p. 519) A commentary is now begun from a very brief text.
This narrative, consisting of questions and answers between Śāṇḍilya and Atharvan, is intended for the praise of this knowledge (*vidyā*).
He introduces the narrative with the words "Śāṇḍilya. Why? [Because he asked], "The Self" (ātman). Thus.

Being questioned by Śāṇḍilya, he said: "What is that? Yoga is said to have eight limbs—namely, *yama*," etc. 2. Definition of the ten-fold *yama*: Among these, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), truthfulness (*satya*), non-stealing (*asteya*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), compassion (*dayā*), straightforwardness (*ārjava*), forbearance (*kṣamā*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), and moderation in food (*mitāhāra*)—

And the purifications; thus, there are ten *yamas*. Among these, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) consists in never causing affliction to any living being at any time through actions of mind, speech, or body. Truthfulness (*satya*) consists in speaking what is beneficial and true regarding beings through actions of mind, speech, or body. Non-stealing (*asteya*)...

Non-attachment is the absence of desire for the property of others through the actions of mind, speech, and body. (7) Celibacy is the renunciation of sexual intercourse in all circumstances, everywhere, through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
(8) Compassion is the bestowing of favor upon all living beings in every way. (9) Uprightness is... [the state of being straightforward]. (10)

Equanimity is the state of being uniform in one's mental, vocal, and physical actions, whether toward those who perform prescribed or prohibited deeds, and whether in engagement with or withdrawal from them. (10) Forbearance is the endurance of all pleasant and unpleasant things, as well as of both physical assault and honor. (11) Steadfastness is [the maintenance of composure] in all circumstances—whether there is loss of wealth, separation from one's beloved kin, or the attainment of them.

The fixing of the mind. || 12 || "Measured diet" means food that is well-oiled and sweet, leaving a fourth part remaining. || 13 || "Purity" is twofold: external and internal. Among these, the external is [attained] by means of earth and water.
Purity of mind is internal; it is to be attained through the science of the self (adhyātmavidyā). 14.
Thus ends the first section,
the description of the ten-fold discipline: austerity, contentment, faith, charity, worship of the Lord, hearing the established doctrines, modesty, intelligence, and recitation.

The observances (*vratas*) are ten restraints (*niyamas*). Among them, austerity (*tapas*) is the emaciation of the body through the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other penances prescribed by the rules. Contentment (*saṃtoṣa*) is satisfaction with whatever is obtained by chance. Faith (*āstikya*) is [belief] in the dharma and adharma declared in the Vedas.

Faith. || 4 || Giving (dāna) means the distribution, with faith, of wealth, grain, and so forth acquired through righteous means to those who seek it. || 5 || Worship of the Lord (īśvarapūjana) means the worship of Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others according to one's ability, with a serene disposition. || 6 ||

7. "Hearing the established doctrine" (siddhāntaśravaṇa) means inquiry into the meaning of the Vedānta. 8. "Modesty" (hrī) means shame regarding despicable actions on the Vedic or worldly paths. 9. "Intelligence" (mati) means faith in the paths of action prescribed by the Vedas. 10. "Recitation" (japa) means...
The practice of mantras according to rule consists of reciting mantras that are not contrary to the Vedas as instructed by the guru. This is twofold:
vocal and mental. Mental practice is that which is joined with meditation through the mind.
Vocal practice is twofold, distinguished by being loud or whispered. Recitation aloud yields the result as previously described.

Whispered recitation is a thousandfold more effective; mental recitation is ten millionfold. (10) A vow (*vrata*) is the constant adherence to the injunctions and prohibitions declared in the Vedas. (11)
Having described the nature of *yama* as divided tenfold, he likewise states the nature of *niyama*:
"Asceticism" (verse 1.9). "Mental" means the contemplation of the meaning of the mantras (verses 1.10–11).
Thus ends the second section:
the description of the eightfold postures.
The postures known as Svastika, Gomukha, Padma, Vīra, Siṃha, Bhadra, Muktaka, and Mayūra—
The eight [postures]: the one named Svastika—
having properly placed both soles between the knees and the thighs.
Sitting with the body straight, that is declared to be the Svastika posture. || 1 ||
One should place the right ankle on the left side of the back, and likewise the left ankle on the right; this is the cow-face posture (gomukha), just as the face of a cow is turned.
One should bind [the hands] with the thumbs and with both hands in reverse order;
having placed both soles of the feet upon the thighs, O Śāṇḍilya, this becomes the Padmāsana, which is honored by all. (3)
Placing one foot upon one thigh and likewise the other thigh upon the other [foot], thus standing, is declared to be the vīrāsana posture.
Placing the right ankle over the left and likewise the other [left] over the right, and having placed both hands upon the knees with the fingers extended; (5)
With mouth open, one should gaze at the tip of the nose with a well-composed mind;
this is the lion-posture (siṃhāsana), always honored by yogins.
Pressing the perineum with the left foot and placing the right foot above the penis,
with the mind focused between the eyebrows— this shall be Siddhāsana.
One should place the two ankles below the scrotum, on either side of the perineal seam;
having bound the sides of the feet firmly with the hands so that they are perfectly motionless,
this shall be the Bhadrāsana posture, which removes all diseases and poisons.
Having pressed the subtle *sīvinī* [artery] on the left side with the left ankle, and the right [side] with the right ankle, this becomes the *muktāsana*. (9)
Firmly supporting the earth with the palms of both hands,
one should place the elbows of the two hands at the sides of the navel.
With the head and feet raised, standing in the sky like a staff—
this is the peacock posture (mayūrāsana), which destroys all sins.
All diseases within the body are destroyed; poisons are digested. Whatever posture allows for comfortable maintenance, one who is unable [to maintain the prescribed posture] should practice that. 13.
He describes the eight types of postures, beginning with the *svastika*, in the verse beginning with "svastika. || 1 ||
He describes the cow-mouth posture (gomukhāsana) with the words "the right" (savya), etc. (2). He explains the lotus posture (padmāsana) with the words "with the big toe" (aṅguṣṭhena), etc. (3).
He states the definition of *vīrāsana*: "One... (verse 4). He describes the method of *siṃhāsana*: "The right... (verses 5–6).

He explains the nature of *siddhāsana*: "The *yoni*... (verse 7). He describes *bhadrāsana*: "The two ankles... (verse 8). He describes the method of *muktāsana*: "Having pressed... (verse 9). He describes *mayūrāsana*:
"Having taken hold," thus [ends verse] 10-13.
The fruit of conquering the posture:
by him who has conquered the posture, the three worlds have been conquered. || 14 ||
A person engaged in the practice of the restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and postures (āsana) should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma). By that, the channels (nāḍīs) become purified. 15.
He states the fruit of mastering the postures with the words "by which" (yena) [verse 14]. To the question "What follows from that?", he says "yamaniyama... [verse 15].
Thus ends the third section. Inquiry regarding the number of the channels and so forth:
Then Śāṇḍilya questioned Atharvaṇ: "By what means [are] the channels [known]?"

"May they become pure. How many are the channels (nāḍīs), and what is their origin? How many vital airs (vāyus) reside within them? What are their locations? What are their functions? Tell me all that which is to be known regarding the body. || 1 ||
Śāṇḍilya, seizing upon the seed of the question, asks the Atharvaṇa; thus he says: "Now," etc. (1).
Regarding the measurement of the body and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), Atharvan said this: "Now, this body consists of ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
the vital breath exceeds the body by twelve finger-breadths. (2)
Thus questioned by Śāṇḍilya, he replied: "It is ninety-six [cubits] according to the measure of one's own fingers. || 2 ||

Regarding the method of breath retention (kumbhaka): he who, through the practice of yoga, makes the vital breath residing within the body equal to or less than the fire becomes a preeminent among yogis. || 3 ||
The meaning is that by the two words "equal" (sama) and "less" (ūna), the kumbhaka and the long kumbhaka are respectively denoted. || 3 ||
The locus of fire within the bodies of humans and other beings is the place of the flame; for humans, it is triangular and has the luster of molten gold,
for quadrupeds it is square, and for birds it is circular.
In its center stands a beautiful, slender flame of fire.
(p. 524) He states the location of the fire for humans and others: "In the body," etc. (4).
The characteristic of the center of the body for humans and others is as follows:
for humans, the middle of the body is two finger-breadths above the secret place (guhya) and two finger-breadths below the penis; for quadrupeds, it is the middle of the heart.
The middle of the belly of birds is nine finger-breadths in length;
it is four finger-breadths in height and breadth, shaped like a water-jar (maṇḍa). || 5 ||
He states the characteristic of the middle part of the body of humans and others, beginning with "from the anus": || 5-7 ||
The soul revolves within the navel-cakra;

the navel is at its center. Therein lies a wheel endowed with twelve spokes. Within that wheel, impelled by merit and demerit, the soul revolves. It is like a gnat situated in the midst of a web of threads.
Just as it revolves, so does that vital breath (prāṇa) move therein; in this body, the individual soul (jīva) becomes mounted upon the vital breath.
The nature and activities of Kuṇḍalinī: the location of Kuṇḍalinī is across from and below the navel.
The Śakti Kuṇḍalinī exists coiled eightfold, having the form of the eightfold primordial nature (aṣṭaprakṛti).
Having properly restrained the movement of the vital air and the flow of water, food, and so forth around the shoulders and sides,

and having encircled this [body] with the mouth, at the time of yoga, she— extremely radiant— throbs through the apāna and fire toward the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) in the space of the heart.
She becomes the embodiment of knowledge. || 8 ||
He states its essential nature and its activity with the words "eight" and "with the tail at the aperture of Brahmā. (8)
p. 525) There are fourteen principal channels; relying upon the Kuṇḍalinī situated in the center, there are fourteen main channels:
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, Suṣumnā, Sarasvatī, Vāruṇā, Pūṣā, Hastijihvā, and Yaśasvinī.
The fourteen channels are Viśvodarā, Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, Payasvinī, Alambuṣā, and Gāndhārī. || 9 ||
Regarding the phrase "situated in the middle of the body": as to what they are, it is *iḍā*. || 9 ||

Therein lies the Suṣumnā nāḍī; the Suṣumnā is the sustainer of the universe, and they call it the "path to liberation. Located at the back of the anus, it rests upon the spinal column (vīṇādaṇḍa) and extends to the head as the Brahma-randhra.
The manifest and the subtle are indeed to be known as belonging to Viṣṇu. || 10 ||
He describes the nature of the Suṣumṇā: "Of the anus," etc. (10).
Regarding the locations of the other channels surrounding the Suṣumṇā:
on the left side of the Suṣumṇā stands the Iḍā, and on the right side stands the Piṅgalā.
The Moon moves within the Iḍā, and the Sun within the Piṅgalā. The Moon is of the nature of darkness (tamas).
The sun is of the nature of *rajas*; the sun is the portion of poison, while the moon is the portion of nectar. These two alone sustain all things at all times. Suṣumnā becomes the enjoyer of time.
On the back and sides of Suṣumnā are Sarasvatī and Kuhū.

Vāruṇī is established between Yaśasvinī and Kuhū. Payasvinī is between Pūṣā and Sarasvatī. Yaśasvinī is between Gāndhārī and Sarasvatī. Alambuṣā is in the middle of the bulb (kanda), in the eastern part of Suṣumṇā.
The *kuhū* reaches as far as the penis. Below and above the *kuṇḍalinī*, the *vāruṇī* extends everywhere. The *yaśasvinī* and *saumyā* are held to extend to the tips of the big toes.
The *piṅgalā* moves upward and reaches the tip of the southern nostril. Behind the *piṅgalā*...
The channel ending at the southern eye is Pūṣā; the one ending at the southern ear is Yaśasvinī;
the one ending at the upper part of the tongue is Sarasvatī; the one going upward from the left ear is Śaṅkhinī; and the one going from the back of the Iḍā to the left eye is Gāndhārī.

From the root of the anus, the lambusā vessel extends both downward and upward. Within these fourteen vessels, other vessels arise; it should be understood that within those others, yet more arise. Just as the leaf of an ashvattha tree or similar plant is pervaded by veins, so too is the body pervaded by channels.
He states that the *iḍā* and other channels stand surrounding the *suṣumnā*: "Of the *suṣumnā*...

[referring to] the locations, movements, and functions of the ten vital airs (*vāyu*), beginning with *prāṇa*—namely, *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*, as well as *nāga*, *kūrma*, *kṛkara*, and *devadatta*.
These ten Dhanañjayas, the vital airs, circulate within all the channels. || 12 ||

The *prāṇa* circulates through the mouth, nose, throat, navel, the two big toes, the *kuṇḍalī*, and the lower and upper parts [of the body]. The *vyāna* circulates through the ears, eyes, hips, ankles, nostrils, throat, buttocks, anus, penis, thighs, knees, abdomen, testicles, waist, calves, and navel.

The apāna wind moves within the rectum and the fire-chamber (the stomach). The udāna wind resides in all the joints. The samāna wind is all-pervading throughout the feet, hands, and all the limbs; it distributes the essence of the food consumed along with the bodily heat through the seventy-two thousand channels.
Moving with the equalizing wind (*samānavāyu*) together with fire, it pervades the body along with its limbs and sub-limbs.

The five winds, beginning with *nāga*, arise from the skin, bones, and so forth. The water and food situated in the stomach are impelled into the [five] tastes and other constituents; the *prāṇa* located within the middle of the stomach shall separate them.

Having placed water above the fire and having arranged food and other offerings upon the water, one draws in the apāna breath oneself; together with that very breath, the wind proceeds toward the flame situated within the body.
The fire, fanned by the wind and driven by the apāna, slowly blazes within the body. The fire [blazes] with its flames.
By means of *prāṇa*, it makes the water located within the cavity of the abdomen exceedingly hot.
It cooks the food placed upon the water along with its condiments by means of that water conjoined with fire.
Through this, *prāṇa* separates the sweat, urine, water, blood, semen, flavors, feces, and so forth.

Pervading the *rasa* (nutritive essence) through all the channels (*nāḍīs*) together with the *samāna* wind, the *vāyu* moves within the body in the form of breath. Through the nine apertures of the body, the winds effect the discharge of feces, urine, and so forth. Exhalation, inhalation, and coughing are said to be the functions of the *prāṇa*.

The function of the *apāna* wind is the expulsion of feces, urine, and so forth; the function of the *vyāna* wind is activities such as abandoning and grasping; the function of the *udāna* wind is the upward movement of the body and so forth; the function of the *samāna* wind is the nourishment of the body and so forth; the function of the *nāga* wind is belching and so forth; and the function of the *kūrma* wind is the closing of the eyes and so forth.
Causing hunger is the function of *kṛkara*; drowsiness is the function of *devadatta*; and phlegm and so forth are the function of *dhanañjaya*. || 13 ||
Having described the classification of the channels, he states the classification of the vital airs: "prāṇa... (verse 12).
He describes the activity of the vital breaths and so forth with the words "of the mouth" (āsya), etc. (verses 13–14).
The Procedure for Purifying the Channels:
Having thus correctly understood the locations of the channels, the locations of the vital airs (vāyu), and their functions, one should perform the purification of the channels. || 14 ||
Thus ends the fourth section:
the characteristics of the person qualified for yoga and the yoga-ashram.
A person who is endowed with the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), free from all attachments, and possessed of realized knowledge.
Delighting in truth and righteousness, having conquered anger, devoted to the service of his guru, obedient to his father and mother,
and instructed by the learned in the virtuous conduct prescribed for his own stage of life, he reaches a penance grove provided with fruits, roots, and water;
in a beautiful location resounding with the chanting of the Vedas and surrounded by those who know Brahman and are devoted to their own duty.

In a temple of the gods well-supplied with fruits, roots, flowers, and water, or on a riverbank, or in a village or city, having constructed a very beautiful hermitage that is neither too high nor too low, not too long, with a small door, smeared with cow dung and the like,
and provided with all protective measures, one should practice yoga while listening to the Vedānta there.
One should begin.

He describes the characteristics of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) along with its varieties and methods, both general and specific, beginning with the word "yamena. Having stated the characteristics of one qualified for yoga, he describes the characteristics of the yoga-shed (*yogamaṭha*) beginning with the word "phale," and [the following] therein, in that yoga-shed. || 1 ||

The method for commencing *prāṇāyāma*: First, having worshipped Vināyaka and bowed to one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the wise practitioner— having mastered his posture— should sit upon a soft seat in the previously mentioned posture, facing either east or north.

Gazing at the orb of the moon between the eyebrows, the tip of the nose, the forehead, and the eyes, one should fill the body with air through the *iḍā* for twelve measures; then, while holding it in the abdomen,

one should meditate upon [the breath] as being joined with a garland of flames, endowed with the syllable *raṃ* and the bindu, and accompanied by the circle of fire (*agni-maṇḍala*), and finally exhale.
Again, having filled [the breath] through Piṅgalā and performed the kumbhaka, one should exhale through Iḍā. || 2 ||
He describes the method for commencing yoga: "At the beginning," etc.; visualizing the lunar disc dripping with nectar. (2)

The duration for practicing breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) to purify the channels (*nāḍī*) is as follows: for three, four, three, four, seven, three, and four months respectively; one should perform it six times—three times at the junctions [of day and night] and three times in the intervals—and thus the purification of the channels occurs. (3)
Regarding how long this should be performed, he states the limit: "three or four," etc.
This means for a period of thirty-three, thirty-four, or forty-three days; or for three, four, or five months, or four months, or seven months;
or up to three or four months, or up to a year. Thus...
For one who performs breath control (prāṇāyāma) six times a day, purification of the channels (nāḍīśuddhi) occurs. || 3 ||
Then, the signs of the purification of the channels occur: lightness of the body, radiance, an increase in digestive fire, and the manifestation of the internal sound (nāda). || 4 ||
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "From that. The meaning is that lightness, radiance, beauty, and so forth arise for the body of the yogi. || 4 ||
Thus ends the fifth section:
Prāṇāyāma consists of the union of prāṇa and apāna, having the nature of the Praṇava.

It is threefold, distinguished by exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka). These [three] consist of phonemes; therefore, the *praṇava* alone is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
He describes the nature of breath control (prāṇāyāma) whose essence is the syllable Om (praṇava): "Prāṇa... etc. (verse 1).
They are the exhalations (recaka) and so forth; because the exhalations and so forth consist of the syllables A, U, and M.
The method of meditating on the syllable *praṇava*:
A person seated in the *padmāsana* or other postures, whose form is covered by a canopy of moonlight from the orb of the moon at the tip of the nose, [visualizes] a red-bodied [deity].

Gāyatrī is a young woman who rides a swan, holds a staff in her hand, and has a white body. Sāvitrī is a young woman who is the embodiment of the syllable *U*, rides a Tārkṣya bird, holds a discus in her hand, and has a white body. The embodiment of the syllable *Ma* is a mature woman with a black body, who rides a bull and carries a trident.
She becomes Sarasvatī. || 3 || She becomes the syllable Om (praṇava), the supreme light, the single syllable that is the cause of all three beginning with the letter 'A'. || 4 ||

The yogin, endowed with the means of accomplishment as previously described, should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the rules, preceded by meditation on the three forms beginning with Gāyatrī, which are denoted by the three syllables beginning with 'A'. Thus he says: "In the lotus... (verse 3).
He states that the aggregate of the three measures (mātrās) beginning with the letter 'a' constitutes the Praṇava: "beginning with 'a'," etc.
[The word] "praṇavam" refers to the essential nature of the Praṇava. || 4 ||
The method for practicing *prāṇāyāma*:
having inhaled air from the outside through the *iḍā* while meditating on the syllable *A*,
one should retain the filled air for sixty-four *mātrās* while meditating on the syllable *Oṃ*.
One should fill [the vessel] with the thirty-two mātrās of Piṅgalā through the meditation on the form of the letter Ma; in this manner, one should perform it again and again in succession. || 5 ||
He describes the method for practicing breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the words: "By means of the iḍā," etc. (verse 5).
Thus ends the sixth section, page 531.

Now, for the purpose of purifying the impurities of the *suṣumṇā*, [the practitioner performs] breath control (*prāṇāyāma*): the yogi, firm in his posture, self-controlled, and moderate in eating wholesome food, [proceeds].

For the purpose of drying up the impurities residing in the *suṣumnā* channel, the yogi, having assumed the bound lotus posture (*baddhapadmāsana*), fills the breath with the moon (*candra*) and retains it according to his capacity; then, exhaling through the sun (*sūrya*), he fills again with the sun and retains it, and exhales through the moon. Having filled [the breath] by means of that same [nostril] through which he had exhaled—
One should retain [the breath]. Regarding this, there are these verses:
One should drink the vital air (prāṇa) through the iḍā first, restrained; then one should exhale it again through the other [nāḍī].
Having drunk the wind through the piṅgalā, one should then bind it and release it through the vāmā.
For those self-controlled practitioners who constantly perform this practice regarding the sun and the moon, the multitude of channels become purified after three months. || 1 ||

The yogi should perform *prāṇāyāma* according to the method previously described for the purpose of purifying the impurities within the *suṣumnā*; thus he says, "Now" (*atha*). He states that the verses to be spoken regarding the aforementioned subject matter constitute *mantras*: "That" (*tat*), etc. (1).
One should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) daily;
specifically, one should perform eighty slow kumbhakas four times each— at dawn, midday, evening, and midnight.
To the question of how many breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should be performed day after day, he says: "In the morning," etc. (2).

In the lowest stage of the restraint of breath (prāṇarodha), there occurs a distinction of success appropriate to practice, namely perspiration; in the middling stage, trembling occurs; in the highest stage, one rises up, and the lotus posture (padmāsana) is attained.
One should perform a massage of the body with water produced from physical exertion;
thereby, firmness and lightness arise in that body. (4)

He explains the distinction between the accomplishments (siddhi) appropriate for practice by saying "the lesser" (kanīyasī) [verse 3]. To the question "What would result from that?", he says "by water" (jalena) [verse 4].
Regarding the regulation of diet during the period of practice:
at the beginning of practice, a diet of milk and ghee is recommended;
once the practice has become stable, there is no such restriction on food.
He states the rule regarding food: "Through practice," etc. (Verse 5).
The rule for attentiveness during practice is as follows:
Just as a lion, an elephant, or a tiger becomes submissive gradually, so too does the vital air (vāyu) when practiced; otherwise, it destroys the practitioner. (6)
One should exhale the breath when it is properly controlled, and one should inhale when it is properly controlled;
one should bind [the breath] with what is properly controlled—thus one shall attain perfection.
"One should practice with vigilance until the entry into the *suṣumnā*";
therefore, he says "as follows" (verse 6). Regarding that, the means is "properly. For one who practices in this manner, the purification of the channels (*nāḍīśuddhi*) occurs (verse 7).

From the purification of the channels, the state of Manonmanī is attained; there is the ability to retain the breath for as long as desired, the kindling of the internal fire, the manifestation of the inner sound (nāda), and health arises from the cleansing of the channels. (8)
When the wheel of channels has been purified by means of the breath-restraints according to rule, the vital air enters easily, piercing the opening of the *suṣumnā*. (9)
When the vital air moves through the middle channel, steadiness of mind arises;
that state in which the mind becomes perfectly steady is itself the state of *manonmanī*.

Then he says that the vital air (vāyu), having entered the *suṣumnā*, shall cause the yogin to ascend to the state of *manonmanī*: "As desired" (yatheṣṭa) || 8-9 || Regarding what would result from that, he says: "The wind" (māruta) || 10 ||
The necessity of performing the three bandhas:

At the end of the inhalation (pūraka), the bandha called Jālandhara should be performed; at the end of the retention (kumbhaka) and at the beginning of the exhalation (recaka), the bandha called Jālandhara should be performed. (11)
By quickly contracting [the perineum] from below when the constriction of the throat is performed,
and by applying a backward stretch in the middle, the vital breath (prāṇa) shall enter the Brahma-nāḍī.
He states that practice preceded by the three bandhas alone is fruitful: "At the end of pūraka," etc. (11–12).
The fruit of the yoga of prāṇa and apāna:
by raising the apāna upward and drawing the prāṇa down from the throat, the yogi becomes free from old age and attains the age of sixteen. (13)
He states the fruit of the yoga of prāṇa and apāna: "Apānam... (verse 13).
The method for purifying the skull:

Seated in a comfortable posture, one should draw the external air through the right channel (nāḍī) up to the tips of the hair and nails, retain it within (kumbhaka), and then exhale it through the left channel. By that [means]:
The purification of the skull results in the destruction of all diseases located within the channels of the vital winds. || 13-1 ||

He states the means for purifying the skull: "In a comfortable posture. The yogi, seated in a comfortable posture, performs the purification of the skull. To the question, "What happens by that? he replies: "The wind... (13-1).
Ujjāyī prāṇāyāma:

having slowly drawn in air through both nostrils with sound from the heart up to the throat, and having retained it as long as possible, one exhales through the *iḍā* [left nostril] while walking or standing.
One should perform it; by that, phlegm is removed and the digestive fire is increased. || 13-2 ||
He states the characteristics of *ujjāyī*, which removes phlegm: "From the heart," etc.
Standing, one should perform the breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) named *ujjāyī*. (13-2)
The *sītkāra-prāṇāyāma*:

having drawn in air through the mouth preceded by the sound *sīt*, one should retain it for as long as possible and exhale through both nostrils. By this, hunger, thirst, laziness, and sleep do not arise.
He describes the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) involving the sound "sīt" with the words "by the mouth," etc. (13-3).
The cooling breath-control (śītalaprāṇāyāma):
having drawn in air through the tongue and retained it as long as possible, one should exhale through both nostrils.
By this, abdominal tumors, spleen disorders, fever, bile, hunger, and so forth are destroyed. (13-4)
But Śītalī is performed with the tongue. || 13-4 ||
The two types of breath retention (*kumbhaka*) consist of the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*).

That *kumbhaka* is of two kinds: *sahita* (accompanied) and *kevala* (isolated). That which is joined with exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*) is *sahita*; that which is devoid of those is *kevala*. One should practice the *sahita* until the mastery of the *kevala* is attained.
When the *kevalakumbhaka* is mastered, nothing in the three worlds becomes difficult for him to attain.
From *kevalakumbhaka*, the awakening of the *kuṇḍalinī* arises. (13-5)

He states the two types of *kumbhaka*—the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*)—in the verse beginning with "In *kumbhaka*. To the question, "What arises from that? he replies with "Only... (verse 13.5).

Then, as a result of the practice of *kumbhaka*, one becomes lean of body, with a serene countenance and clear eyes; the internal sound (*nāda*) becomes manifest, the web of diseases is cast off, the vital drops (*bindu*) are mastered, and the digestive fire becomes sharp. (13.6)
Regarding the question "What would follow from that?", [the text says] "from that" (tataḥ). || 13-6 ||
The attainment of the Vaiṣṇavī Mudrā:
the inner focus with the gaze directed outward, free from blinking or opening the eyes—this is that Vaiṣṇavī Mudrā, hidden in all the Tantras. (14)

In response to the inquiry "What is the result of that?", he states: "The internal object" (*antarlakṣyam*), meaning that by this [practice], the yogi becomes established in the Vaiṣṇava mudrā. The internal object refers, respectively, to the Virāṭ, the Sūtra, the Bīja, or the Turya, located in the Mūlādhāra, Anāhata, Ājñā, and Sahasrāra [cakras].

The meaning is that when the mind, which is otherwise directed outward, becomes inwardly focused and remains free from the opening and closing of the eyes, then this very vision becomes the Vaiṣṇavī Mudrā. || 14 ||
Through the attainment of Khecarī, the yogi— whose mind and vital breath have dissolved into the internal object of focus— always abides in the vision of Brahman;
with a gaze of unwavering pupils, looking outward and downward, he sees yet does not see.
This indeed is the Khecarī mudrā; it is auspicious, focused one-pointedly on the object of perception, and free from both void and non-void; it vibrates as the reality, the very state of Vaiṣṇavī.
With eyes half-closed, mind steady, and gaze fixed on the tip of the nose,
he brings even the sun and moon to a state of dissolution; then, beyond the state of flowing [nectar],
there is the supreme light-form, devoid of all externality, intensely radiant.
O Śāṇḍilya, know that the ultimate reality here is that supreme entity which is the object [of meditation].

When the yogi has ascended to the Vaiṣṇavī-mudrā, then this Vaiṣṇavī-mudrā, having reached the state of Khecarī, becomes directed toward Brahman as non-different from the inner self—the unity of the referents of the terms *tattvam* and *padam*. Thus he says: "Within... (antar).
This is the *mudrā* wherein the external gaze remains motionless, having attained the state of the internal gaze.

The meaning is that the Vaiṣṇavī [power] flashes forth as one-pointed concentration on the objective, such that it is void like deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and non-void like dreaming (*svapna*) and so forth, while being free from both. || 15 ||

He describes the state of the yogi established in the *khecarīmudrā* and the nature of that which is to be meditated upon with the words beginning with "half-closed": "The yogi, characterized by such attributes as having his eyes half-open, [unites] the moon and the sun—
the breaths moving through the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*— within the *suṣumnā*, together with the mind, the gaze, and the fire."

When one remains while inducing a state of absorption (*līnatā*) or the condition of dissolution (*layabhāva*), then the river of the bliss of Brahman— which causes one to forget both the internal and the external— flows forth. Thereafter, following that state of outflow (*niṣyandabhāva*), after the experience of the intensely flowing state of bliss, [the following occurs].

O Śāṇḍilya, there exists that supreme reality, established by the scripture which states, "The light beyond the heavens shines," which is the inner luminous form, free from all internal and external mental constructs due to its non-attachment to their experience, and which blazes intensely through its non-difference from the Supreme Self.
Know that the object which has attained that state, having that as its sphere, is "I am Brahman. || 16 ||
Through Khecarī, one attains the state of Unmanī: having joined the breath (tāra) with the light, slightly raise the eyebrows;
this is the path of prior practice that brings about Unmanī in an instant. (17)
Therefore, one should practice khecarīmudrā. From that, the state of unmanī arises; from that, the state of yogic sleep (yoganidrā) arises.
For the yogi who has attained yogic sleep, time does not exist. || 17-1 ||
To explain how this can be known, he states the means: "the pupil" (*tāram*).
Having firmly united and gazed upon the pair of black pupils that have attained a state of equilibrium within the light shimmering between the eyebrows, [one should look] slightly...

Having raised the eyebrows upward and performed an upward projection, one should then perceive—by means of the intellect that remains as its own self—the fourth state shining in the *sahasrāra*, or that which transcends the fourth (*turiyatīta*) due to the cessation of its mental activity;
this is the implied meaning. This is the internal object of focus (*antarlakṣya*) which was shown by the instruction: "having joined the *tāra* with the light."

The meaning is that this very path is the cause for the attainment of the state of non-conceptual Brahman, which brings about the *unmanī* state in an instant for one who has such prior practice as described above. Since this is so, therefore [it follows].
"Then it becomes *unmanī*" means that the mind (*manas*) becomes free from activity. To the question "What happens then?", he says:

Regarding the word "tataḥ": *yoganidrā* is the attainment of a state free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa-bhāvāpatti*). He wards off the suspicion of emerging from that state by saying "labdha" (attained). Thus, for the yogi who has attained *yoganidrā*, there is no time of emergence from that state of non-conceptualization. 17-1.
Having placed the mind within the Śakti as the means for attaining Brahman which is unconditioned by time, and having placed the Śakti within the mind;
and having perceived the mind with the mind, O Śāṇḍilya, be happy. 18.
Place yourself within the void, and place the void within yourself;
having made everything consist of the void, do not think of anything at all.
He describes the means for attaining the state of non-conceptual Brahman, which is undivided by time:

having fixed the mind within the Kuṇḍalinī energy and having dissolved the mind, [one should focus] on that Kuṇḍalinī energy— and because of the word "ca" (and)— on the gaze, both situated in the middle of the mind.
Having brought [the mind] to rest within the immediate consciousness that is the cause of the mind's activity,
one perceives with the mind that has attained the state of inwardness—
that very mind which is non-different from Brahman, the inner self that illumines the existence and non-existence of the thousands of mental modifications.

"Having perceived [the Self] as 'I am ashes'—O Śāṇḍilya, the meaning is that you should become one who experiences the bliss of liberation (kaivalya), characterized by abiding in those subtle elements alone. || 18 ||

He states another method: "In the middle of the sky," and so forth. Place the self—the internal organ—within the sky of consciousness (*cit-kha*), and place the sky within the self and the internal organ. Thus, by means of this mutual exchange (*vyatihāra*), having made everything consist of the sky of consciousness, contemplate that nothing exists apart from the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). 19.
Through the stilling of the mind, one attains absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
One should not engage in external thought, nor likewise in internal reflection.
Abandoning all thought, become intent solely upon pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). (20)
Just as camphor dissolves in fire and rock salt in water,
so too the mind, being dissolved, merges into the principle of reality (tattva).
All that is to be known is universally perceived, and that knowledge is called the mind;
when knowledge and the object of knowledge have equally vanished, there is no other second path.
When the objects of knowledge are relinquished, the mind dissolves;
when the mind has dissolved, absolute liberation remains.
Since the vision of space arises in some way for one who is veiled by external and internal mental fluctuations,

he says "external" [in verse 20]. This is because the realization of non-dual pure consciousness (cinmātra) is preceded by the negation of the conceptualization of the distinction between internal and external.

He says "camphor" to show that at the very moment of awakening to the impossibility of any commonality in the objects of knowledge, the yogi remains as the nature of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*): like burnt camphor or a lump of rock salt dissolved in water, the mind dissolves into the three states beginning with waking.

Having become purified by meditation on its own nature and turned away from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it dissolves into Brahman, which is its own true essence (*svatattva*). [Objection: Since the mind consists of the phenomenal world, its objects, the knowable, and the act of knowing, how can it dissolve into its own true essence? To this, he says: "The knowable... [and so forth]. This means that [the mind] perceives everything as being distinct from itself.
This is universally recognized. By the term "the sphere of ignorance" (*avidyāpada*), the phenomenal expansion of waking and its effects is denoted;
all of that is the meaning of the word "the knowable" (*jñeya*). The mind whose object is that [phenomenal expansion] is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
At the very moment of the realization that "there is nothing whatsoever apart from Brahman," knowledge and the knowable [become one].

It becomes lost simultaneously and at once; the meaning is that this alone is the path leading to the non-dual Brahman, and there is no other whatsoever. (22) To the question, "How does it dissolve simultaneously?", he says:
"The knowable... (23).

p. 539) Through yoga and knowledge, there is the dissolution of the mind; there are two methods for the destruction of the mind, O Lord of Sages: yoga and knowledge. Yoga is indeed the cessation of mental fluctuations, while knowledge is right discernment. || 24 ||
When that [mind] has been ceased, the mind will surely become tranquil;
through the cessation of the mind's vibration, saṃsāra dissolves away. || 25 ||

Just as worldly activity ceases when the vibration of sunlight subsides, one might ask: how then is the mind dissolved? Anticipating this doubt, [the text states that] the mind is dissolved through the practice of yoga and knowledge directed toward Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman).
He states [the answer] with an illustration: "Two," etc. Yoga is the cessation of the mental fluctuations that take as their object the existence of anything other than oneself;

knowledge (*jñāna*) is the correct discernment that nothing exists apart from Brahman. (24) While that delusion which arises [in the form] "there exists something other than myself" persists, and while *saṃsāra* exists, how can the mind [be stilled]?

Regarding the phrase "it becomes tranquil," the word "mind" (*mana*) is implied. The expression "with the cessation of the mind's vibration" (*manaḥspandopaśāntyāyām*) means "upon the cessation of the mind's vibration. There is also an alternative reading: *manaḥspandopaśāntyāyam*. [In this state,] transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) dissolves; [this refers to] the dissolution of transmigratory existence.
The meaning is that because [the world] is imagined by the mind, the absence of the object of imagination is logical when the imaginer is absent. (25) Here is the illustration: "sūrya... etc.

From the dissolution of the mind, there occurs the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath, through the study of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, detachment, practice, and yoga. || 26 ||

When one has first established detachment from the activities of saṃsāra and instead cultivated attachment [to liberation], through long-term meditation on the desired object arising as a single unity; 27.

Through firm practice on a single reality (*ekatattva*), the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) is restrained, because the vibration of the mind—which is conceptualized by one's own ignorance—is preceded by the vibration of the vital breath. Since this is so, the means for its cessation is stated as "the teaching" (*śāstra*). [Verse 26] Regarding non-attachment (*anāsthā*):
When firm conviction has been established in the path of cessation (nivṛttimārga), the knowledge arises that Brahman is real and the world is illusory.
Thereafter, "just as... (yathā) || 27 ||

From the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath comes the cessation of the vibration of the mind, through the firm practice of breath-restraints such as inhalation (pūraka) and so forth, performed without fatigue. || 28 ||
And through the yoga of one-pointed meditation, the vibration of the mind is restrained.
Regarding how the vibration of the mind is stilled, it is said here: "By means of inhalation," etc. (28).
"At the very moment the vibration of the vital breath ceases, that is the mind."
Through various means for the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), by experiencing the reality of the sound at the limit of the utterance of the syllable *oṃ*,
when consciousness becomes like deep sleep, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained. (29)
Having diligently pressed the uvula with the tongue so that it reaches the root of the palate,
when the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the upper aperture, the vibration of the breath is restrained.
When consciousness has dissolved into the vital breath and the breath reaches the upper limit of twelve finger-breadths above the palate,
the vibration of the breath is restrained through the upper aperture by means of practice.
When the vision of consciousness becomes tranquil at the tip of the nose— twelve finger-breadths away in the stainless ether— the vibration of the vital breath is arrested.
When the light of the star [the mind] has reached its cessation between the eyebrows, and consciousness is bound in a single focus, the vibration of the vital breath is restrained. (33)

When that auspicious knowledge, which is identical with the object of knowledge, arises as the very syllable "Om," the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is restrained, being untouched by any part of modification.

O Sage, through the long-term realization of the sky-like absolute within the heart, and by means of meditation on a mind free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained. (35)
By these methods, as well as others devised through various conceptualizations and residing in the mouths of various teachers, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇaspanda) is brought to cessation.
He states that even through the contemplation of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) as it is being dissolved, the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is restrained:

"By the sound of *Oṃ*," etc. This means by contemplating the resonance of the *praṇava*, which, like the ringing of a bell made of white-metal (*kāṃsya*), persists after the initial utterance. [This restrains] the consciousness of internal and external existence—that is, the entire expanse of objective cognition.

When deep sleep has arisen, then [the breath] moves through the *prāṇa*—thus it is said. He states that even by means of the *lambikā*, there may be the cessation of the vibration of the *prāṇa*: "The palate," etc. By means of that method, [the breath] goes to the upper aperture (*ūrdhvarandhra*). || 30 ||
Through proficiency in the practice of *rājayoga*, [one attains] the vital breath (*prāṇa*). When consciousness has dissolved by means of the *ṣaṇmukhī* mudrā—
such that the mental construction of external and internal consciousness has vanished— through practice,
the *prāṇa* [proceeds] from the upper opening of the palate to the *dvādaśānta* (the "twelve-finger limit") shining above the palate.

When the thousand-spoked wheel has been reached, then [one practices] "prāṇa" (breath-control). || 31 || He states that mastery over the vital breath (*prāṇa*) may also be achieved through external *kumbhaka* (retention): "twelve," etc. When the perception of consciousness is becoming tranquilized, and when the mental fluctuations directed toward objects other than itself have ceased. || 32 || Also, by means of the contemplation of the Star (*tāraka*).

Between the eyebrows; when the peace resulting from the gazing at the star (the point between the brows) has been attained; when the resolve "the gazing at the star must be performed" has reached its conclusion; then, when the mind has become one-pointed in consciousness—that is, when it is bound in one-pointedness within the conscious inward-facing Self—and having thus entered the state of *manonmanī*, then [the breath] moves through the *prāṇa*. || 33 ||

He says "Om" to indicate that even through the knowledge of Brahman, there occurs the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa-spanda). And he says that very thing: "I am all that, liberated—Om.
Simultaneously with the knowledge of the portion untouched by modifications, which arises from the investigation of the meaning of the syllable Om, [liberation occurs].
"Prāṇa... (34). He states that through meditation and the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there occurs the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*):

"For a long time," etc. Through the perception of the solitary void within the heart—that is, from the knowledge that nothing exists apart from the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoman*)—the latent impression is destroyed. Consequently, the mind becomes focused solely upon the object of meditation.

The meaning is that there shall be the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). He states—by the words "by these"—that through the means already mentioned or those not yet mentioned, when practiced for a long time, the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath occurs. || 36 ||

By means of *kumbhaka* (retention), through the piercing of the *suṣumnā*, one proceeds to the supreme state; having opened the door of Kuṇḍalinī by means of contraction (*ākuñcana*), one should break open the gate of liberation.
That door by which one must go is covered by her mouth. (36–1)
The sleeping Kuṇḍalinī, coiled like a serpent, exists in a curved form.
That power (śakti) by which she is awakened becomes liberation. If that Kuṇḍalinī is asleep in the region above the throat, it leads to the liberation of yogins; [if] below, it leads to bondage.
For the deluded: having abandoned the two paths beginning with Iḍā, one should proceed by way of the Suṣumṇā;
that is the supreme station of Viṣṇu.

The yogi, through the practice of *kevala-kumbhaka* characterized by the cessation of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), should pierce the entrance to the *suṣumnā* via the *kuṇḍalinī*. Thus it is said: "By contraction...
[He] should pierce the door of the *suṣumnā*, the gateway to liberation, the *brahmarandhra*. (36–1)
He describes the nature of Kuṇḍalinī, which pierces the doors to liberation, and the fruit of its movement, beginning with the words "by which."
36-2,3 || Because it is thus, [it is called] "beginning with *iḍā*"; for the *suṣumnā* is the gateway to reaching the station of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇupada*).
The method for the entry of the life-force (prāṇa) conjoined with the mind into the suṣumnā:
one should practice all the exercises of the vital air (marut) joined with the mind;
the wise person should not allow the activity of the mind to go elsewhere. (37)
One should not worship Viṣṇu by day, nor indeed should one worship him at night;
one should worship Viṣṇu constantly, neither by day nor by night.

The meaning is that the practice of mental yoga is fruitful. He says "by day" to indicate that one should cause the vital breath (prāṇa), joined with the mind, to engage upon the Great Path (mahāpatha) without allowing it to enter the two paths beginning with Iḍā. Through the union of the mind, [one reaches] Viṣṇu, the vital breath.

During the day, one should not worship nor engage [the breath] in the solar channel (*sūryanāḍī*); likewise, at night, one should certainly not worship in the lunar channel (*candranāḍī*). Therefore, one should worship Viṣṇu within the great path known as Suṣumnā, which is filled with the unmanifest space (*avyākṛtākāśa*) and is ever-present.
The meaning is that one should never fail to worship, whether by day or by night. || 38 ||
The attainment of Khecarīmudrā is a hollow aperture that generates knowledge and is endowed with five channels;
O Śāṇḍilya, Khecarīmudrā resides there, so indeed practice it. 39.
When the vital breath (māruta) moves through the middle, situated in both the left and right channels, the khecarī mudrā remains in that place; of this there is no doubt.
One should swallow the void and the *ali* between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*;
there the *khecarī* mudrā abides, and therein truth is established. (41)
Furthermore, situated upon the supportless surface between the moon and the sun,
within the wheel of space (vyomacakra), she is known by the name Khecarī Mudrā.

Anticipating the question, "What would result from entering the *suṣumnā*?", [the author] states "In the cavity" (*suṣire*), indicating that the *khecarīmudrā* exists therein; through its direct realization, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. In that center of the *suṣumnā*, there is a cavity (*suṣira*) endowed with the five currents beginning with the *virāj* and ending with the *turīyātīta*.

In the mūlādhāra, anāhata, ājñā, and sahasrāra cakras, this [state] sequentially becomes the generator of the knowledge of Virāṭ and the other forms for the yogin; therein alone exists the khecarīmudrā, which is of the nature of the non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka). The meaning is: "By my grace, you should cultivate that. To reiterate the aforementioned point:
He clarifies this further with another expression: "savye" (verse 40). By the word "void" (śūnya), the unmanifest space (avyākṛtākāśa) is meant, because space is swallowed by the wind (verse 41).
Because the celestial wheel (vyomacakra) is without support. || 42 ||
The means for attaining the external *khecarī* [siddhi]:

Having made the tongue the supreme *kalā* through cutting, moving, and milking, and having fixed the gaze between the eyebrows, when the tongue enters the hollow of the skull in a reversed manner, then—
The Khecarī Mudrā is produced. The tongue and the mind move in the void (kha). Therefore, a man whose tongue is turned upward becomes immortal. || 42-1 ||

He states the means for attaining the external *khecarī* [siddhi] with the words "cutting," etc.: every day, for a period of six months, by cutting the veins of the tongue by a hair’s breadth with a blade resembling the leaf of the *snuhī* plant,
and by moving the tongue during every *brāhma-muhūrta*, [one should consume] in the morning a powder of rock salt (*saindhava*) and *pathyā*.

Having made the tongue extremely subtle with the supreme art (*kalā*) of *dohās*, and having fixed the pair of eyes between the eyebrows, when the tongue enters the hollow of the skull through the aperture of the uvula (*ghaṇṭikārandhra*) in a reversed manner, then the *khecarīmudrā* arises; by the entry of the tongue into the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*), the yogi [attains this state].
The meaning is that one has accomplished what was to be done. || 42-1 ||
The method for conquering the vital breath (*prāṇa*) during the time of practice:
pressing the perineum (*yoni*) with the root of the left foot, extending the right leg and holding it with both hands, filling the nostrils with air, and performing the throat-lock (*kaṇṭhabandha*).

Having drawn [the breath] upward, one should hold the wind; by that, there is the destruction of all afflictions (*kleśa*). Then, even poison is digested like nectar. Disorders such as consumption, abdominal tumors, intestinal obstructions, and skin ailments are destroyed. This is the means for mastering the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which destroys all death. (42–2)
He states the means for conquering the vital breath (*prāṇa*) at the time of practice: "By the left," etc.; by that [means], namely through the practice of *mahāmudrā*. (42-2)
The means for the direct realization of one's own self:
having placed the heel of the left foot at the site of the *yoni*, having positioned the right foot upon the left thigh,
having filled the breath, having placed the chin against the heart, and having contracted the *yoni*.
Having held [the mind] within the center of the mind according to one's capacity, one should contemplate one's own self;
by that, direct realization is attained. 42-3.
He states the means for the direct realization of one's own Self: "Vāma," etc. One should contemplate one's own Self as "I am Brahman. Thus, realization occurs. (42–3)
A specific method of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) for liberation from all diseases:
having drawn the breath from the outside and filled it, one should [hold it] with effort in the middle of the belly, at the center of the navel, at the tip of the nose, and on the big toe. (43)
One should restrain the vital breath (prāṇa) with the mind during the periods of twilight or at all times;
thus the yogi shall be liberated from all diseases and freed from fatigue.
He states a specific type of *dhāraṇā*: "From the external," etc. (vv. 43–44).

Through *saṃyama* on the tip of the nose and other locations, various supernatural powers (*siddhis*) arise. By [concentration] on the tip of the nose, mastery over the vital air (*vāyu*) is attained. In the center of the navel, there is the destruction of all diseases.
From fixing [the mind] on the big toe of the foot, lightness of the body occurs. (44–1)
The man who, having drawn in the wind through the *rasanā*, drinks it constantly, shall experience neither fatigue nor burning heat, and likewise his diseases shall perish. (45)
The Brāhmaṇa who, at the time of the two twilights, draws in and drinks the air,
for him a beautiful speech, Sarasvatī herself, arises within three months.
Thus, through practice for six months, there is the cessation of all diseases.
Having drawn in the breath with the tongue, one should restrain it at the root of the tongue.
The wise man who drinks this nectar attains every auspiciousness. (47)
Having held the self within the self by means of the iḍā at the space between the eyebrows,
one who pierces the food of the gods is liberated even while afflicted by disease.
Having drawn the vital air (vāyu) through the two channels into the navel, he who holds it there at the sides of the abdomen for one ghaṭikā is liberated from diseases. || 49 ||
Having placed the breath upon the tongue during the three junctions of the day for one month,
and having pierced through the food of the thirty [gods], one should hold it in the middle of the abdomen.
All fevers and various poisons are destroyed for one who constantly,
even for a moment, fixes the mind together with the intellect upon the tip of the nose.
One overcomes all afflictions accumulated over hundreds of births through restraint upon the *tāra* (the syllable Om).

Through restraint of the mind upon the *tāra*, knowledge of all objects arises. Through restraint of the mind upon the tip of the nose, there is knowledge of the world of Indra. Through restraint of the mind below that, there is knowledge of the world of Agni.

From *saṃyama* on the mind in the eye comes knowledge of all worlds; from *saṃyama* on the mind in the ear, knowledge of the world of the immortals (*amara-loka*); from *saṃyama* on its side, knowledge of the world of Nirṛti; from *saṃyama* on the back part, knowledge of the world of Varuṇa; [and] in the left ear...
From *saṃyama* on the throat, there is knowledge of the world of Vāyu; from *saṃyama* on the neck, knowledge of the world of Soma;
from *saṃyama* on the left eye, knowledge of the world of Śiva; from *saṃyama* on the head, knowledge of the world of Brahmā; [and from *saṃyama*] on the lower part of the feet...
Through *saṃyama* on the soles of the feet, there is knowledge of the world of Talātala; through *saṃyama* on the feet, knowledge of the world of Vitala;

through *saṃyama* on the ankles, knowledge of the world of Nitala; through *saṃyama* on the calves, knowledge of the world of Sutala; and through *saṃyama* on the knees, knowledge of the world of Mahātala.
By restraining the mind on the thighs, there is knowledge of the world of Rasātala;

by restraining the mind on the hips, there is knowledge of the world of Talātala; by restraining the mind on the navel, there is knowledge of the world of Bhūrloka; and by restraining the mind on the belly, there is knowledge of the world of Bhuvarloka.

Through *saṃyama* on the mind in the heart, there is knowledge of the world of the gods (*svarloka*). Through *saṃyama* on the mind in the upper part of the heart, there is knowledge of the Maharloka. Through *saṃyama* on the mind in the throat, there is knowledge of the Janoloka.
Through *saṃyama* on the mind between the eyebrows, there is knowledge of the Tapoloka. Through *saṃyama* on the mind in the head...

Knowledge of the world of truth (*satyaloka*). Through *saṃyama* on dharma and adharma, knowledge of the past and future. Through *saṃyama* on the mind with respect to the sounds of various creatures, knowledge of the minds of all creatures. Through *saṃyama* on accumulated karma, knowledge of previous births. Through *saṃyama* on another's mind...

Knowledge of the minds of others; by restraining the mind upon the form of the body, one perceives invisible forms. By restraining the mind upon strength, one attains the power of Hanumān and others. By restraining the mind upon the sun, one gains knowledge of the worlds.
By restraining the mind upon the moon, one gains knowledge of the arrangement of the stars. By restraining the mind upon the pole star (*dhruva*), one perceives their movements.

From *saṃyama* on one’s own nature comes knowledge of the *puruṣa*. From *saṃyama* on the navel-center comes knowledge of the arrangement of the body. From *saṃyama* on the hollow of the throat comes cessation of hunger and thirst. From *saṃyama* on the tortoise-channel (*kūrmanāḍī*) comes steadiness. From *saṃyama* on the *tāra* (the point between the eyebrows) comes vision of the perfected ones (*siddhas*). From *saṃyama* on the body and space comes the power of moving through space. [This occurs] in each respective location.
From self-restraint, those respective perfections arise. || 52 ||
He states that various supernatural powers (*siddhis*) arise from *saṃyama* (concentration) on the space beginning with the tip of the nose and ending with the body:
"At the tip of the nose" [refers to] by means of retaining the breath at the tip of the nose (44–47). "By the tongue" [refers to] by means of the tongue (45–47).

Having pierced the lunar orb and drunk the nectar, the food of the thirty [gods], he who perceives the target together with the mind—[this occurs] through the restraint of the stars; that is, through the restraint of the mind upon the stars (the *tāraka*), this applies everywhere. [The word] "in the shanks" means in the shanks. Such is the perfection [attained].

If it is argued that [siddhi] is a means to achieve the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), we say no, because such accomplishment is an obstacle to those very goals. For there is no knowledge of one's own or another's body, nor of the fourteen worlds and their objects, apart from [the Self]. Therefore, the meaning is that seekers of liberation (mumukṣu) should not honor the path of supernatural powers (siddhi). || 52 ||
Thus ends the seventh section:
the fivefold withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra). Now, regarding withdrawal: it is fivefold with respect to the objects [of the senses].

Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is the forceful drawing back of the wandering senses. Pratyāhāra is perceiving that whatever one sees is all the Self. Pratyāhāra is the renunciation of the fruits of obligatory duties. Pratyāhāra is turning away from all sense objects. [It is practiced] in the eighteen vital points (*marmasthāna*).

Successive retention is *pratyāhāra*. || 1 || The locations are the big toe, the ankle, the calf, the knee, the thigh, the waist, the genitals, the navel, the heart, the throat, the pit of the throat, the palate, the nose, the eyes, the space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and the crown of the head. One should perform *pratyāhāra* upon these, in successive order, by means of ascending and descending. || 2 ||
Having explained the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), postures (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the incidental teachings on the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*),

and the various supernatural powers (*siddhi*) that are its adversaries, he now describes the withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), which is the subject at hand among the limbs of yoga, with the word "atha" (now): "from their respective objects by force."
Successively: retention, withdrawal, transference, and retraction.
(1) Regarding the question "What are the vital points?", [the answer is] "The foot," and so forth. (2)
Thus ends the eighth section. Now, the fivefold meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*): that [concentration] is fivefold; the fixing of the mind upon the self (*ātman*).
The concentration on the external ether within the internal ether, and the concentration on the five forms in earth, water, fire, air, and ether.
He is fivefold; they are fivefold. This is the bearing of the five Brahmans and the five forms.
Thus ends the ninth section. Now, regarding meditation (*dhyāna*): meditation is of two kinds, namely, with attributes (*saguṇa*) and without attributes (*nirguṇa*). [The first is] with attributes...
Meditation on the Form; the essential nature of the Self as devoid of qualities.
For the true nature of the Self consists solely in the remainder of the Self alone, established by the negation of the non-self.
Thus ends the tenth section.
Now, the nature of Samādhi: Samādhi is the state of oneness between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman), devoid of the threefold division [of knower, known, and knowing].
She is of the nature of supreme bliss and consists of pure consciousness.
The individual soul (jīva) has the subtle ignorance (tūlāvidyā) as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), while the Supreme Self (paramātman) has the root ignorance (mūlāvidyā) as its limiting adjunct.

When the portions of these adventitious distinctions have ceased, the identity of the inner self and the supreme self shines forth; this state of the oneness of the individual self and the supreme self is what is meant by being "of the nature of the non-conceptual" (nirvikalpakarūpin).
Since one might ask, "If the triad exists, how can there be non-conceptuality? he says: "The triad...

Because it devours the modifications such as the triad, which are the transformations of the nature of non-conceptuality, [the state] would otherwise be of the nature of suffering in the absence of the triad;
therefore, he says: "Supreme Bliss... This refers to the state of non-conceptuality that devours the suffering of the triad.

Fearing that the state of oneness might be insentient because its nature is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), he declares it to be pure consciousness by virtue of being the form of *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*, stating: "Pure... Here, the term "the state of oneness of the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*)" refers to *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*.
This is the meaning.
Thus ends the eleventh section;
this is the first chapter.
The second chapter.

Now, indeed, the Brahman-sage Śāṇḍilya, not having obtained the knowledge of Brahman in the four Vedas regarding the nature of Brahman which is without distinction, [asked] Atharvaṇa: "What is its name?"

Having approached the Blessed One, he asked: "Teach me, O Blessed One, the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), by which I may attain the highest good. He, Atharvan Śāṇḍilya, said: "Brahman is truth, consciousness, and infinite."

Having heard the truth of one's own Self even through the pretext of the eightfold yoga, yet failing to realize it as it truly is, Śāṇḍilya asks Atharvan again out of a desire to know the knowledge of Brahman alone—which is non-dual and devoid of distinctions—as expressed by the word "atha" (now). This is stated as follows: "Even though the Vedas have been determined in their meaning..."

[He asked about] the knowledge of Brahman alone, which is without a counterpart. "What indeed is Brahman? he asked. "Teach me," [he said], "by means of your instruction. (1) Thus questioned by Śāṇḍilya, he spoke. To the question, "What indeed is Brahman? the answer was: "Śāṇḍilya! [It is] Truth, Consciousness, and Infinite."
This has been correctly explained in the Taittirīyaka as "Brahman. || 2 ||
The indefinability of Brahman:
That in which this [universe] is woven across and lengthwise, that in which all this comes together and dissolves,
and by the knowledge of which all this becomes known— that is without hands or feet, without eyes—
It is without ears, without tongue, without body; ungraspable and indefinable. || 3 ||
He says that whatever is the substratum of all is indefinable—referring to the phrase "in which":

this entire collection of the state of ignorance and its effects, having attained the condition of being woven warp and woof therein, undergoes contraction and expansion; and by the knowledge of that alone, this [world] is seen as nothing other than oneself.

It is known; that very thing, established by the negation of the body consisting of the individual and collective aspects of hands, feet, and so forth, is "indescribable" because it cannot be pointed out as a reality. || 3 ||
Brahman is beyond the range of speech and mind,

since words turn back from it along with the mind without reaching it; that which is accessible solely through knowledge, from which the ancient wisdom has issued forth, and which is one without a second.

Like space, it is all-pervading, extremely subtle, stainless, actionless, pure existence, the singular essence of consciousness and bliss, auspicious, profoundly peaceful, immortal, and that supreme Brahman.
"That art thou"—know this indeed through the knowledge of That. 4.
He states that it is beyond the range of speech and mind, accessible through knowledge alone, the generator of wisdom, non-dual, and in reality nothing but existence-consciousness-bliss—
by the words "yataḥ" (from which). The meaning is that it is accessible solely by knowledge and inaccessible by any means other than knowledge.

According to the Vedic scripture, "There is no other path for going," that non-conceptual state consisting of pure consciousness is called *prajñā*. This ancient wisdom (*prajñā*) is established by the Vedas, as it persists until the state of final liberation (*kaivalya*). It is from her that [this world] has issued forth and expanded.

That which is pure consciousness (caitanya-mātra), which—when confronted with transformations such as duality—is qualified by terms like "non-dual" (advitīya) and so forth, and in the absence of those [transformations] is pure Being (san-mātra), according to the Śruti: "Everything else is non-existent";
that which remains as the non-relational pure Being established through the negation of all that is non-existent—that alone is it.
The meaning is: "Understand that there is nothing else apart from all that. || 4 ||
The state of being the supreme Self of all belongs to that one God who is preeminent in His own power, the omniscient Lord of all,
the inner Self of all beings, the abode within all beings, and hidden within all beings.
The source of all beings, attainable through yoga alone; he who creates the universe, sustains the universe, and enjoys the universe—that is the Self. Know that very world to be within the Self. 5.

But how can everything be known by that [knowledge] alone, given the existence of a creator Lord (Īśvara) who is distinct from that Brahman? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: he who appears as a separate Lord through the vision of one ignorant of oneself (svājña-dṛṣṭi) is, in fact, through the vision of one who knows oneself (svajña-dṛṣṭi), that very [Brahman] itself.
He says "he who" (yaḥ) to indicate that [the Self] remains as the Supreme Self:

he for whom *prakṛti*—meaning the power consisting solely of the Self established through the negation of the non-Self—is primary (*pradhāna*) and principal, while the powers of being a witness, lordship, and so forth, are subordinate (*upasarjana*). He is this very one.
He is primarily characterized by the power of the Self; by relying on subordinate powers, He is omniscient, and so forth.

Since the direct realization of God is achievable through Yoga alone, [the author] states the inferential mark for the existence of God with the words "And he who... That whose mark is the universe—that is my Self, without a doubt.
Having understood the existence of the Lord through the indirect definition established by the scriptures,

you should realize that whatever is designated as the Lord, the Witness, the individual soul (jīva), or the world— once the superimposed distinctions attributed by the ignorant have been removed— is in reality nothing but the non-dual Brahman alone, devoid of all counter-correlates. || 5 ||
Through the instruction of the Guru, one attains the knowledge of being the Self of all:
"Do not grieve; as one who has realized the Self, you shall reach the end of sorrow. (6)

"Do not grieve, thinking, 'How can this be known?'—by the power of my instruction, you shall become Brahman, the end of the sorrow born from the existence of anything other than yourself," he says: "Do not grieve. (6)
Thus ends the second chapter.
The third chapter:
Brahman’s state of being, in reality, its own non-dual self alone.

Then Śāṇḍilya questioned Atharvan: "How is it that from that single syllable (akṣara), which is actionless, auspicious, pure existence alone, and the supreme Brahman, this universe is born? How does it abide? And how is it dissolved therein? [Please resolve] this doubt of mine."
"You ought to cut it away," [he said]. Atharvan replied, "O Śāṇḍilya, the Supreme Brahman is indeed reality;
it is actionless and imperishable."

(p. 553) It has been stated that Brahman is its own self alone, devoid of any counterpart, and that from it the universe is born. However, if Brahman is its own self alone, devoid of any counterpart, its being the cause of the universe is not possible; and if it is the cause of the universe, its being devoid of any counterpart is not possible. Thus, there arises a desire to know the extent of that which is distinct from Brahman.

Śāṇḍilya asks Atharvaṇ; thus he says: "Now" (atha) || 1 || Brahman, however, has pure Being (sanmātra) as its material cause; without that non-relative self-material cause, it does not undergo the modifications of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe. [This occurs] due to the lack of knowledge regarding its true nature (tattva). It is devoid of [such change].
He spoke this answer to the question of Śāṇḍilya, who was filled with doubt: "O Śāṇḍilya,

that which I have described as Pure Being, the Supreme Brahman, which is without a counterpart and established through the negation of all objective existence— including the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, as well as the transformations of cause and effect— is to be trusted."

That alone is the supreme, the imperishable, and the truth. There is no doubt regarding its state of being without a counterpart, for whether the delusion of the perspective of one's own ignorance exists or not, it remains as the singular form of the Self. || 2 ||

Now, regarding the three forms of Brahman: although Brahman is formless, it possesses three forms—namely, the partless (niṣkala), the with-parts (sakala), and the both-with-and-partless (sakalaniṣkala). || 3 ||
If that is so, one might ask: "From where does its status as the cause of the universe arise?

Anticipating this doubt, he states that although Brahman is partless and devoid of any counterpart, it appears—as if with a counterpart—as partless, as with parts, and as both with and without parts, due to the diversity of the ultimate perspectives of those who know themselves and those who do not know themselves.
Now, "atha" (then). || 3 ||
That which is the partless Brahman—
truth, consciousness, bliss, actionless, stainless, all-pervading, extremely subtle, facing in all directions, indefinable, and immortal— is this very same partless [reality].
Form. || 4 ||

Let that which is described from the perspective of ultimate reality as "without counterpart" and "partless" remain as it is— for the realization of that state is preceded by the negation of all relative conceptualizations; rather,
pure consciousness alone is consciousness, the undivided single essence, the very flavor of being.
Pure consciousness alone, devoid of everything, is Brahman alone; it is indeed not non-existent.

...from such scriptural passages as these (p. 554). Therein, first of all, relying on the perspective of one’s own realization (*svajñadṛṣṭi*), he clarifies the partless essential nature (*niṣkalasvarūpa*) which possesses a counter-correlate (*sapratyayika*), beginning with the words "That which... (*yad iti*).
This is because the aforementioned qualifiers—such as "being," "knowledge," and "bliss"—function as the negation of untruth, insentience, suffering, and so forth.

The state of having a counter-correlate (sapratiyogikatva) is logical; however, in the view that there is no counter-correlate, even the delusion regarding whether the general category of objects to be negated exists or does not exist has itself been sublated. || 4 ||
The Absolute (Brahman) is thus "with parts" (sakala).

Furthermore, that innate knowledge which belongs to it—Māyā, the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), which is red, white, and black—the Lord Maheśvara, being endowed with that [innate power], rules as the dark-brown (kṛṣṇapiṅgala) one. This, then, is his state of being "with parts."
Form || 5 ||
He clarifies the form that possesses a counter-correlative (*sapratiyogika*): "Now" (*atha*).

That which remains as the non-dual (*niṣpratiyogika*) and partless (*niṣkala*) is itself known as the "partless with a counter-correlative" (*sapratiyogika-niṣkala*) from the perspective of one's own ignorance (*svājñadṛṣṭi*). That very same [reality], immediately following conceptualization (*vikalpa*) from the perspective of one's own ignorance, becomes the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*).

To the question "What is the cause of His lordship? he says: "By which. The Lord is possessed of that innate Māyā, consisting of the three *guṇas*, which is introduced as the Root Nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) from the perspective of those who lack self-knowledge; through union with the three *guṇas*, Maheśvara—being dark and tawny—rests upon universal lordship.
He presides over the collection of his own ignorance and its effects, which are attached to the vision of those who do not know themselves.

This is His form as the *sakala* (the conditioned). However, because the Lord possesses the powers of action, knowledge, and will that are free from obscuration, and because—according to His own vision—He is devoid of the state of ignorance and its effects that would otherwise be objects of His lordship, He is Himself non-dual and without a counterpart.
The meaning is that because this [Reality] is partless, its appearance as having parts is based solely upon the perception of those who lack self-knowledge. || 5 ||
Brahman, both with parts and without parts, then, being built up by the austerity consisting of knowledge, desired: "May I become many;
may I procreate. Then, from Him as He was performing austerity, three syllables were born.
The three *vyāhṛtis*, the three-footed *gāyatrī*, the three Vedas, the three gods,
