the three castes, and the three fires are born. That Lord who is the Divine One,
endowed with all sovereignty, all-pervading, and seated in the heart of all beings—
The Illusionist, whose form is illusion—he is Brahmā, he is Viṣṇu, he is Rudra, he is Indra;

he is all the gods, he is all beings. He alone is in front, he alone is behind, he alone is to the north, he alone is to the south, he alone is below, he alone is above; he alone is everything. Now, of him—

The beautiful body of the God who sports with his own power and is compassionate toward his devotees—Dattātreya—is clothed in blue garments resembling the petals of a blue lotus; he has four arms, is non-terrible, and does not manifest evil.
This is his form, both with parts and without parts.

Having established the perspective of one who knows half [of the truth], he explains the nature of both the *sakala* (with parts) and *niṣkala* (without parts), preceded by a detailed exposition of his own essential form, beginning with the word "Now" (*atha*). That in which the *sakala* is seen at the beginning and the end, while the *niṣkala* is seen in the middle, is the nature of the *sakala-niṣkala*. In that regard, although Īśvara is one...
Being built up and growing by means of austerity (*tapas*), he formed the resolve to become manifold and to procreate, thinking, "May I be many. Thus,
from that Lord (*Īśvara*) whose resolve is true, [the syllables arise] through the distinction of *a*, *u*, and *m*.
The phrase "three syllables were born" is to be applied everywhere in accordance with the scriptural statement.

There are three *vyāhṛtis* distinguished as *bhūḥ* and so forth; the *gāyatrī* consisting of three feet; the three Vedas distinguished as *Ṛg* and so forth; the three gods distinguished as Brahmā and so forth; and the three social classes distinguished as the Brāhmaṇa and so forth.

Furthermore, the three fires—the Gārhapatya and the others—arise through such distinctions. This very Lord, endowed with limitless majesty, is all-pervasive by virtue of his nature as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) and resides within the hearts of all beings. His possession of form is due to *māyā*, not inherently; inherently, he is formless.
Because he is formless; yet he exists even in the form of Brahmā and others. He alone exists in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, below, and above.

He exists even in the form of Dattātreya. From the qualifying description "beautiful-bodied and unclothed," his state as an Avadhūta is understood, [as seen in the cases of] Jaḍabharata, Dattātreya, and Raivataka.

According to the scripture stating "Rbhu and Nidāgha," the meaning is that the nature of both the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala) has been thus established in accordance with the perspective of one who knows half of himself. || 6 ||
Thus ends the first section, the definition of pure Being as the Supreme Brahman.
Now, Śāṇḍilya questioned Atharvaṇ: "O Venerable One, [what is] pure Being?"
"Why is that which has the singular essence of consciousness-bliss called the Supreme Brahman? Atharvan replied:
"Because it is great (*bṛhati*) and causes all things to grow (*bṛṃhayati*), therefore it is called the Supreme Brahman."

Śāṇḍilya asks Atharvan how it is that Brahman possesses the nature of pure existence (sanmātratva), the state of the Supreme Brahman (parabrahmatva), the state of the Self (ātmatva), and the state of the Great Lord (maheśvaratva);
and he states that the venerable Atharvan likewise provided the answer to those questions— beginning with "Now" (atha).
Why is it merely existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda) without a counterpart? 1-8.
The definition of the Self as pure Being:
Now, why is it called the "Self" (ātman)? Because it pervades everything, because it takes up everything, and because it consumes everything;
therefore it is called the Self.
The definition of the state of Maheśvara for the Pure Being (sanmātra) is as follows:
Now, why is it so called? Because he is the Lord (īśa) of the Great (mahat), by means of his own power consisting of the resonance of sound (śabdadhvani), therefore he is called Maheśvara.
The definition of the True Being as Dattātreya:
Now, why is he called Dattātreya? Because, when Atri—who was performing extremely difficult penance and desiring a son—was exceedingly gratified, his very Self, consisting of light, [was given].
Because he was given to Anasūyā and became the son of Atri, he is therefore called Dattātreya. || 8 ||
Now, the fruit of knowing the etymologies:
he who knows its etymologies knows everything. Now, he who indeed worships this supreme one with the knowledge "I am He" becomes a knower of Brahman.
In this regard, there are these verses:
One should meditate upon the Lord Dattātreya—auspicious, peaceful, resembling a sapphire, the God who delights in his own *māyā*, the ascetic (*avadhūta*) clad in the directions as his garment. (11)
The Lord, whose entire body was smeared with ashes, who wore a mass of matted locks,
who possessed four arms and noble limbs, and whose eyes were like full-blown lotuses.
The treasure-house of the yoga of knowledge, the teacher of the universe, beloved by practitioners of yoga,
compassionate toward devotees, the witness of all, and served by the perfected ones (siddhas).
Thus, he who constantly meditates upon the eternal God of gods shall be liberated from all sins and attain the supreme beatitude.
Thus, "This is the truth," is the Upaniṣad. 15.

He states the fruit of knowing the three [terms] whose etymologies have been explained, beginning with "Now" (atha). The meaning is that because Brahman is all-pervasive, through the knowledge of Brahman, one becomes all-knowing. || 9 || He says, beginning with "Now," that he who, having known this Brahman, meditates upon it, becomes that very thing; "vidya" means having known.

10–13 || He who, having understood the God of gods, the Supreme Self, in the manner thus described as "I am this," should meditate upon Him, shall attain that state of supreme beatitude. 14 || That which is Truth, shining at the tip of the syllable Om, is indeed that very [state].
The meaning is "it becomes. Thus, the word "Upaniṣad" marks the conclusion of the Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad. || 15 ||
Thus ends the second section, and the third chapter as well.

This commentary on the Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad, which has Brahman as its subject matter, was written by Upaniṣad-Brahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra. The extent of this Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad commentary is recorded as three hundred [verses].
Thus ends the commentary on the Śāṇḍilyopaniṣad, completing the fifty-eighth [treatise] in the exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the venerable Īśa.
